status_reasoning: Reviewers request additional information about patient samples, stating 'please present a table summarizing each patient's age and clinical characteristics.' While the decreased sFLT-1 expression in AMD eyes is shown, the lack of detailed patient characterization raises questions about the robustness of this finding.

Reviewers raise concerns about sFLT-1 localization data, noting 'why does the sFlt-1 IHC look so completely different in Figure 3A compared to Figure 1C?' and asking 'how far towards the inner retina is sFlt-1 reduced?' These inconsistencies in staining patterns and incomplete characterization of expression domains suggest uncertainty about the precise localization claims.

Reviewers express philosophical concerns about reproducibility, stating 'if other scientists fail to reproduce the subretinal injection experiments in which the outcome is CNV volume (e.g., Figures 3B and D), the authors could claim that special skill is required.' They note that injection experiments have inherent weaknesses and 'put more weight on experiments that require no special manipulation.'

Reviewers question the VEGF measurement methodology, asking 'How can the authors be sure that their ELISA does not measure non-free VEGF (bound to sFlt-1)?' and noting 'This is a bit surprising, considering the very high affinity sFlt-1 has for VEGF. The authors should demonstrate that this is possible for VEGF (but not for PlGF) in vitro.'

Reviewers question PlGF data, asking 'how can the authors explain the fact that PlGF is not changed?' and 'can the authors be sure that they are measuring true free PlGF (and not PlGF bound to sFlt-1)?' These questions indicate uncertainty about the mechanistic interpretation regarding PlGF versus VEGF-A.

Reviewers request additional controls for the shRNA approach, asking 'why have they not shown this in the Western blot' to demonstrate that mFlt-1 is not affected, and questioning 'how far towards the inner retina is sFlt-1 reduced?' The lack of complete characterization creates uncertainty about the specificity of the knockdown.

Reviewers acknowledge the AAV-shRNA approach as one of 'three different, independent approaches' and note that 'each one of the three approaches has its weaknesses, but the fact that each approach has the same outcome makes the overall study quite compelling.' The convergent evidence from multiple methods supports these claims despite individual methodological concerns.

Reviewers request a critical control experiment, stating 'A critical control experiment for recombination efficiency and location is needed for the subretinal injection of Cre plasmid' and suggesting injection of mTmG mice to determine 'where and at what efficiency Cre-mediated recombination takes place.' The absence of this control creates uncertainty about the specificity of the Cre-mediated effects.

Reviewers note that the authors 'performed this control for the RPE and photoreceptor-specific lines,' indicating acceptance of the cell-type specificity demonstrated in the transgenic models. No concerns are raised about the Cre expression patterns in these lines.

Reviewers emphasize the importance of these transgenic models, stating 'the reviewers put more weight on experiments that require no special manipulation, in particular the RPE-specific and photoreceptor-specific Flt-1 KOs.' However, they request 'a quantification of the neovascularization events per retina' because 'one cannot tell whether this represents a common or rare occurrence in these eyes,' indicating uncertainty about the penetrance and reproducibility.

Reviewers raise major concerns about CNV quantification methodology, stating 'It is not clear how exactly CNVs were quantified' and 'how can CNVs be distinguished in this image modality from fluid build-up due to leakage?' They note that 'the V in CNV stands for vascularization, yet the authors do not show any vascular specific stains (apart from Figure 4D). This is a major weakness.'

Reviewers request vascular-specific staining, stating 'Why have the authors not used a vessel specific stain to show CNVs? It is impossible to be certain that vascular changes have occurred based on the H&E stains shown.' This indicates uncertainty about the characterization of RAP lesion progression without proper vascular markers.

Reviewers request demonstration of VEGF protein localization changes, stating 'the authors show in Figure 1C VEGF IHC in sections. This stain should be used to demonstrate where the VEGF protein is reduced.' They also question incomplete characterization of sFLT-1 expression changes throughout the retina.

Reviewers request temporal studies, asking 'how quickly do the CNVs develop in the transgenic models?' and noting 'We can't be certain there is not a primary effect (because in these experiments sFlt-1 and mFlt-1 are absent). A temporal study showing early vascular changes in the absence of changes in the transgenic target tissues could exclude this.' The current temporal data is insufficient to rule out primary tissue effects.

Reviewers affirm the overall significance, stating 'this is an important study with significant clinical implications' and 'the fact that each approach has the same outcome makes the overall study quite compelling.' They note the models are 'of general interest' and that the observation of CNV versus RAP depending on cell type is 'even more interesting.'

Reviewers note 'One recurring piece of data is that CNV occurs in the control eyes, although at a lower incidence. It is never addressed why this happens. This should be discussed.' The occurrence of CNV in controls raises questions about the specificity and interpretation of the phenotype frequencies reported.

Reviewers express skepticism about cell-type specificity, stating 'Regarding RPE vs photoreceptor sFlt-1 loss, it is hard to believe that loss of sFlt-1 from one cell type would not be compensated for by diffusion of sFLT-1 made by the other cell type.' This challenges the authors' explanation for why distinct phenotypes arise from different cell types.
